compare_blocks.title: One-minute comparison

compare_blocks.body:
S describes a preference for concrete information and firsthand experience. T concerns how people weigh decisions against consistent criteria. Asking where a number came from can fit either type, and neither preference tells you how thorough or reliable someone will be.

At the letter level, E/I is about where attention and energy tend to go, and J/P concerns whether the outward approach favors settling arrangements or keeping options open. Type dynamics adds a separate distinction: ESTP leads with Se, which attends to what can be observed now, and ISTJ leads with Si, which relates what is happening to remembered experience. Either type can check what is happening on site and consult the records.

### The same on-site information: which basis each takes

Give both the same matter, the same information and the same deadline. ESTP more often takes what can still be observed now — the other person's reaction at this moment, what happens if this step is tried, how far the conditions at hand allow — while ISTJ more often takes what has accumulated: how a similar case was handled last time, which points have been verified, what the record says.

Each has a precondition. Sourcing from the scene pays off in fast feedback, provided trial and error is cheap, reversible and involves no multi-person handover; the cost is possibly missing a pattern visible only in the records. Sourcing from experience pays off in fewer omissions, provided this case resembles the last one closely enough; the cost is that the situation has moved on while the basis stays in the previous round.

Keep the counterexamples: an ESTP who has been through a serious incident may check every point before starting, and an ISTJ against a deadline may fill in records as they go. That is experience, responsibility and risk rewriting the approach, not an exception to a type.

What can be distinguished is not the order of actions but where the answer lands when asked "why did you decide that": "this is what I just saw", or "we did this last time and it is in the record".

### Why the direction of all four function labels reverses

The stacks use different functions in all four positions under the convention used here.

ESTP's P means the outward process is perceiving, and for an E type the outward process sits in the dominant, so the dominant is Se; the auxiliary is the inward judging process Ti. ISTJ's J means the outward process is judging, and for an I type the outward process sits in the auxiliary, so the auxiliary is Te and the dominant is the inward perceiving Si. The two therefore come out as extraverted perceiving with introverted judging, and introverted perceiving with extraverted judging.

Aligned by position, that gives four pairs with the same category and opposite direction: Se against Si, Ti against Te, Fe against Fi, Ni against Ne. So "all the names differ" and "the families still correspond" are two sides of one fact, not two separate rules.

Whether the third position carries a direction label is not consistent across tables: the common version marks a direction for ESTP's Fe and ISTJ's Fi, and some versions give only the function name; when an arrangement differs, check the source, and the disagreement does not change the first two positions.

How alike the two are depends on which layer is asked about. Ask "do they trust data" and both may; ask "where does the data come from" and one more often measures it now, the other more often opens last year's records. A function is a position in the model, not the order of work. Base descriptions are in the [ESTP profile](/en/personality/estp) and the [ISTJ profile](/en/personality/istj).
compare_blocks.title: Why they are easily confused

compare_blocks.body:
Scope note: the two passages below are editorial fictions about the same matter, describing what each may attend to in front of the same information, not who should do what. The division follows who knows how, who is present and who usually handles outward contact, not type; judgements involving safety and professional matters go to help and professional guidance first, and type does not enter them.

### Travelling to see a client tomorrow: one email, two kinds of sourcing

(Fictional scene.) Notice comes late: tomorrow morning, a new client in the next city. The email raises three questions, gives a budget range and does not say whether to bring a demo unit. The information is the same and so is the one evening available.

In this fictional scene, one approach looks at what can still be added on site: call on the way to find out which of the three matters most, adjust the wording to the reaction in the room, book the earliest train and keep margin for a face-to-face conversation. The other takes the existing record: what the last similar client asked, which clauses kept coming up, whether the demo unit was actually used last time, then prepare an answer to each of the three questions and book a changeable ticket. Both types can combine these bases; which step is taken depends on the division of work, the authority and the information available.

The cost depends on conditions. Pushing forward on site pays when the other side changes their mind mid-meeting, provided the trip is mainly reconnaissance and errors are cheap; the cost is arriving to find they wanted a written proposal. Preparing from the record pays in solid answers, provided this client resembles the last; the cost is that the focus has shifted and the preparation is aimed at the wrong thing.

The counterexamples hold as well: an ESTP who has dealt with public-sector clients often brings the full pack, and an ISTJ going to see an old acquaintance may take only a business card — the requirement of the duty outweighs the preference.

One thing worth doing is a review, not a change of method: after the trip, each writes three lines on what was mainly relied on, why it was chosen, and how they would adjust if the client moved the date or the requirement. The difference usually shows in those three lines, not in the size of the bag; and there is no need to repeat the trip several times to settle it.

### Packing to move: one van, the same two pairs of hands

(Fictional scene.) The lease ends and the move must finish on Saturday. One small van, two friends helping, a lift in the building, but the van can only park for ten minutes. The constraint is the same for both.

In this fictional scene, one approach handles the flow on the day: which trip takes the large items, how to stagger the lift, what can be bought after arriving at the new place; a box marked "kitchen" or "misc" is enough to recognise. The other handles the existing information: pack by room, number the boxes, write the contents, mark fragile items separately, load what will not be needed for six months first, and leave one "first night" box at the end. Both types can combine these bases; which step is taken depends on the division of work, the authority and the information available.

The cost follows conditions too. Handling the flow first pays in fewer van trips and a finish on the day, provided the large items are few and anything missing can be bought nearby; the cost is hunting through boxes for a pillow at night. Packing by room first pays in being able to live there immediately, provided there are enough hands and time; the cost is packing until dawn while friends wait downstairs.

A counterexample: people who have moved five times mostly label boxes, and someone living independently for the first time may shove things in anywhere. That relates to experience, hands and the day's energy, with no correspondence to four letters.

The real compromise is a division of work, not persuasion: one sets the van trips, the floor order and the route for large items, the other sets the packing rules and the first-night supplies, and who does which depends on who knows how and who is present. Before starting, both confirm two things — what time the van must leave, and which items must go in last — and the rest of the detail belongs to each.
compare_blocks.title: Illustrative scenarios

compare_blocks.body:
Reading E and I as "outgoing and lively" against "silent and withdrawn" is the easiest step to trip on. ISTJ can talk for a long time among familiar people, and ESTP can go a whole day without seeking anyone out. E and I describe whether attention and energy go outward or inward more often, not social appetite and not expressive ability.

The second misread is taking J and P as "has a plan" and "has none". ESTP will also work out the last train when travelling far, and ISTJ's weekend may have nothing arranged at all. The difference is whether an arrangement is formed outward first or options are kept, not the density of the calendar.

The third slip is ranking by "reliability", or reducing the shared S and T to "only wants data, only gives results". Punctuality, delivery and answering messages belong to habit and responsibility; both types can do all three and both can miss. Both types also cite data and both accept someone else's experience-based judgement; the difference is which is taken first. Using one incident or one catchphrase to overturn a whole set of preferences only describes how someone has been lately.

### Travelling to see a client tomorrow: one email, two kinds of sourcing

(Fictional scene.) Notice comes late: tomorrow morning, a new client in the next city. The email raises three questions, gives a budget range and does not say whether to bring a demo unit. The information is the same and so is the one evening available.

In this fictional scene, one approach looks at what can still be added on site: call on the way to find out which of the three matters most, adjust the wording to the reaction in the room, book the earliest train and keep margin for a face-to-face conversation. The other takes the existing record: what the last similar client asked, which clauses kept coming up, whether the demo unit was actually used last time, then prepare an answer to each of the three questions and book a changeable ticket. Both types can combine these bases; which step is taken depends on the division of work, the authority and the information available.

The cost depends on conditions. Pushing forward on site pays when the other side changes their mind mid-meeting, provided the trip is mainly reconnaissance and errors are cheap; the cost is arriving to find they wanted a written proposal. Preparing from the record pays in solid answers, provided this client resembles the last; the cost is that the focus has shifted and the preparation is aimed at the wrong thing.

The counterexamples hold as well: an ESTP who has dealt with public-sector clients often brings the full pack, and an ISTJ going to see an old acquaintance may take only a business card — the requirement of the duty outweighs the preference.

body: S describes a preference for concrete information and firsthand experience. T concerns how people weigh decisions against consistent criteria. Asking where a number came from can fit either type, and neither preference tells you how thorough or reliable someone will be.

At the letter level, E/I is about where attention and energy tend to go, and J/P concerns whether the outward approach favors settling arrangements or keeping options open. Type dynamics adds a separate distinction: ESTP leads with Se, which attends to what can be observed now, and ISTJ leads with Si, which relates what is happening to remembered experience. Either type can check what is happening on site and consult the records.
### The same on-site information: which basis each takes

Give both the same matter, the same information and the same deadline. ESTP more often takes what can still be observed now — the other person's reaction at this moment, what happens if this step is tried, how far the conditions at hand allow — while ISTJ more often takes what has accumulated: how a similar case was handled last time, which points have been verified, what the record says.

Each has a precondition. Sourcing from the scene pays off in fast feedback, provided trial and error is cheap, reversible and involves no multi-person handover; the cost is possibly missing a pattern visible only in the records. Sourcing from experience pays off in fewer omissions, provided this case resembles the last one closely enough; the cost is that the situation has moved on while the basis stays in the previous round.

Keep the counterexamples: an ESTP who has been through a serious incident may check every point before starting, and an ISTJ against a deadline may fill in records as they go. That is experience, responsibility and risk rewriting the approach, not an exception to a type.
What can be distinguished is not the order of actions but where the answer lands when asked "why did you decide that": "this is what I just saw", or "we did this last time and it is in the record".
### Why the direction of all four function labels reverses
The stacks use different functions in all four positions under the convention used here.

ESTP's P means the outward process is perceiving, and for an E type the outward process sits in the dominant, so the dominant is Se; the auxiliary is the inward judging process Ti. ISTJ's J means the outward process is judging, and for an I type the outward process sits in the auxiliary, so the auxiliary is Te and the dominant is the inward perceiving Si. The two therefore come out as extraverted perceiving with introverted judging, and introverted perceiving with extraverted judging.

Aligned by position, that gives four pairs with the same category and opposite direction: Se against Si, Ti against Te, Fe against Fi, Ni against Ne. So "all the names differ" and "the families still correspond" are two sides of one fact, not two separate rules.

Whether the third position carries a direction label is not consistent across tables: the common version marks a direction for ESTP's Fe and ISTJ's Fi, and some versions give only the function name; when an arrangement differs, check the source, and the disagreement does not change the first two positions.

How alike the two are depends on which layer is asked about. Ask "do they trust data" and both may; ask "where does the data come from" and one more often measures it now, the other more often opens last year's records. A function is a position in the model, not the order of work. Base descriptions are in the [ESTP profile](/en/personality/estp) and the [ISTJ profile](/en/personality/istj).

body: Scope note: the two passages below are editorial fictions about the same matter, describing what each may attend to in front of the same information, not who should do what. The division follows who knows how, who is present and who usually handles outward contact, not type; judgements involving safety and professional matters go to help and professional guidance first, and type does not enter them.
### Travelling to see a client tomorrow: one email, two kinds of sourcing

(Fictional scene.) Notice comes late: tomorrow morning, a new client in the next city. The email raises three questions, gives a budget range and does not say whether to bring a demo unit. The information is the same and so is the one evening available.

In this fictional scene, one approach looks at what can still be added on site: call on the way to find out which of the three matters most, adjust the wording to the reaction in the room, book the earliest train and keep margin for a face-to-face conversation. The other takes the existing record: what the last similar client asked, which clauses kept coming up, whether the demo unit was actually used last time, then prepare an answer to each of the three questions and book a changeable ticket. Both types can combine these bases; which step is taken depends on the division of work, the authority and the information available.

The cost depends on conditions. Pushing forward on site pays when the other side changes their mind mid-meeting, provided the trip is mainly reconnaissance and errors are cheap; the cost is arriving to find they wanted a written proposal. Preparing from the record pays in solid answers, provided this client resembles the last; the cost is that the focus has shifted and the preparation is aimed at the wrong thing.

The counterexamples hold as well: an ESTP who has dealt with public-sector clients often brings the full pack, and an ISTJ going to see an old acquaintance may take only a business card — the requirement of the duty outweighs the preference.

One thing worth doing is a review, not a change of method: after the trip, each writes three lines on what was mainly relied on, why it was chosen, and how they would adjust if the client moved the date or the requirement. The difference usually shows in those three lines, not in the size of the bag; and there is no need to repeat the trip several times to settle it.
### Packing to move: one van, the same two pairs of hands

(Fictional scene.) The lease ends and the move must finish on Saturday. One small van, two friends helping, a lift in the building, but the van can only park for ten minutes. The constraint is the same for both.

In this fictional scene, one approach handles the flow on the day: which trip takes the large items, how to stagger the lift, what can be bought after arriving at the new place; a box marked "kitchen" or "misc" is enough to recognise. The other handles the existing information: pack by room, number the boxes, write the contents, mark fragile items separately, load what will not be needed for six months first, and leave one "first night" box at the end. Both types can combine these bases; which step is taken depends on the division of work, the authority and the information available.

The cost follows conditions too. Handling the flow first pays in fewer van trips and a finish on the day, provided the large items are few and anything missing can be bought nearby; the cost is hunting through boxes for a pillow at night. Packing by room first pays in being able to live there immediately, provided there are enough hands and time; the cost is packing until dawn while friends wait downstairs.

A counterexample: people who have moved five times mostly label boxes, and someone living independently for the first time may shove things in anywhere. That relates to experience, hands and the day's energy, with no correspondence to four letters.

The real compromise is a division of work, not persuasion: one sets the van trips, the floor order and the route for large items, the other sets the packing rules and the first-night supplies, and who does which depends on who knows how and who is present. Before starting, both confirm two things — what time the van must leave, and which items must go in last — and the rest of the detail belongs to each.

- Shared S: both prefer information from concrete facts and first-hand experience. That is a sourcing emphasis; it does not mean rejecting inference, and does not mean accepting only what can be checked on the spot.
- Shared T: both prefer impersonal criteria that can be applied consistently rather than asking first who would be more comfortable. Being able to state a standard does not guarantee the answer is right.
- E/I: the ESTP side, E, turns attention and energy more often to the people and events happening outside; the ISTJ side, I, more often returns to inner sorting and impressions already formed. This describes direction, not how much someone talks, and not whether they can handle social occasions.
- J/P: the ISTJ side, J, more often fixes the timing, the arrangement and the conclusion when facing the outer world; the ESTP side, P, more often keeps options and adjusts to information that arrives. This describes outward stance, not how full the calendar is.

Using the type-dynamics convention on this page, the stacks are: Se–Ti–Fe–Ni for ESTP and Si–Te–Fi–Ne for ISTJ. At each position the category matches and the direction reverses: Se against Si, Ti against Te, Fe against Fi, Ni against Ne. The attitude of the third process is labelled differently elsewhere, and this whole arrangement is a convention adopted here, not the Foundation's only version.

These labels describe emphasis inside the model. They do not predict the order of behaviour, and do not show who is more capable or better suited to a kind of post. On the same move, or the same last-minute trip, either may make the call first, write the list first or start lifting first; order depends more on duty, experience, staffing and deadline.

sections.title: Quick answer

sections.body_md:
S describes a preference for concrete information and firsthand experience. T concerns how people weigh decisions against consistent criteria. Asking where a number came from can fit either type, and neither preference tells you how thorough or reliable someone will be.

At the letter level, E/I is about where attention and energy tend to go, and J/P concerns whether the outward approach favors settling arrangements or keeping options open. Type dynamics adds a separate distinction: ESTP leads with Se, which attends to what can be observed now, and ISTJ leads with Si, which relates what is happening to remembered experience. Either type can check what is happening on site and consult the records.

### The same on-site information: which basis each takes

Give both the same matter, the same information and the same deadline. ESTP more often takes what can still be observed now — the other person's reaction at this moment, what happens if this step is tried, how far the conditions at hand allow — while ISTJ more often takes what has accumulated: how a similar case was handled last time, which points have been verified, what the record says.

Each has a precondition. Sourcing from the scene pays off in fast feedback, provided trial and error is cheap, reversible and involves no multi-person handover; the cost is possibly missing a pattern visible only in the records. Sourcing from experience pays off in fewer omissions, provided this case resembles the last one closely enough; the cost is that the situation has moved on while the basis stays in the previous round.

Keep the counterexamples: an ESTP who has been through a serious incident may check every point before starting, and an ISTJ against a deadline may fill in records as they go. That is experience, responsibility and risk rewriting the approach, not an exception to a type.

What can be distinguished is not the order of actions but where the answer lands when asked "why did you decide that": "this is what I just saw", or "we did this last time and it is in the record".

### Why the direction of all four function labels reverses

The stacks use different functions in all four positions under the convention used here.

ESTP's P means the outward process is perceiving, and for an E type the outward process sits in the dominant, so the dominant is Se; the auxiliary is the inward judging process Ti. ISTJ's J means the outward process is judging, and for an I type the outward process sits in the auxiliary, so the auxiliary is Te and the dominant is the inward perceiving Si. The two therefore come out as extraverted perceiving with introverted judging, and introverted perceiving with extraverted judging.

Aligned by position, that gives four pairs with the same category and opposite direction: Se against Si, Ti against Te, Fe against Fi, Ni against Ne. So "all the names differ" and "the families still correspond" are two sides of one fact, not two separate rules.

Whether the third position carries a direction label is not consistent across tables: the common version marks a direction for ESTP's Fe and ISTJ's Fi, and some versions give only the function name; when an arrangement differs, check the source, and the disagreement does not change the first two positions.

How alike the two are depends on which layer is asked about. Ask "do they trust data" and both may; ask "where does the data come from" and one more often measures it now, the other more often opens last year's records. A function is a position in the model, not the order of work. Base descriptions are in the [ESTP profile](/en/personality/estp) and the [ISTJ profile](/en/personality/istj).

sections.body_md:
Align the conditions first: the same client email, the same vehicle and the same number of helpers, the same deadline and budget. Both types can use both approaches — ESTP will also write the list in advance, and ISTJ will also change the route on the day; the table states which basis is taken first more often under comparable conditions, and when that basis tends to work. If one has done this many times, that column drifts toward expertise and can no longer be used to classify.

| The same matter (same information, hands and deadline) | ESTP: the basis more likely attended to | ISTJ: the basis more likely attended to | What this row illustrates |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| The same client email (three questions, one budget range) | What the email raises, and what can be verified on site | The record left by the last similar meeting, and what can be verified this time | Two complementary Sensing materials; looking now or checking records cannot separate E/I |
| How far the quotation should be prepared | May keep several quotation options open until the same terms are confirmed | May settle on a provisional quotation within the same scope, with unresolved terms marked | J/P: how firmly to settle the same arrangement |
| How to book the travel | Keep two workable departures open while the meeting time is unconfirmed | Agree on a provisional departure and a fallback while the meeting time is unconfirmed | Outward stance: J/P |
| The three optional items in the bag | Whether they can be bought nearby on arrival | Which were used last trip, and whether they are at home | Shared Sensing: either can check the same supplies and past use |
| Someone adds a requirement at short notice | May keep more than one response open while both check the same urgency and scope | May agree on a provisional update to the scope within the same constraints | J/P: how firmly to settle the same arrangement |
| Looking back on the same trip | Sort out with a colleague how I read the change in the meeting | Recall the meeting alone first, noting what needs checking with the colleague | E/I: direction of attention and energy; either may check records and join the discussion |

The differences in the table are not a scale of ability. A column belonging to someone who has made many such trips drifts toward expertise; the same person also changes approach with duty, staffing and deadline, so these rows only suggest which basis may be taken first, and cannot be used to classify.
sections.title: ESTP and ISTJ in one minute

sections.body_md:
Scope note: the two passages below are editorial fictions about the same matter, describing what each may attend to in front of the same information, not who should do what. The division follows who knows how, who is present and who usually handles outward contact, not type; judgements involving safety and professional matters go to help and professional guidance first, and type does not enter them.

### Travelling to see a client tomorrow: one email, two kinds of sourcing

(Fictional scene.) Notice comes late: tomorrow morning, a new client in the next city. The email raises three questions, gives a budget range and does not say whether to bring a demo unit. The information is the same and so is the one evening available.

In this fictional scene, one approach looks at what can still be added on site: call on the way to find out which of the three matters most, adjust the wording to the reaction in the room, book the earliest train and keep margin for a face-to-face conversation. The other takes the existing record: what the last similar client asked, which clauses kept coming up, whether the demo unit was actually used last time, then prepare an answer to each of the three questions and book a changeable ticket. Both types can combine these bases; which step is taken depends on the division of work, the authority and the information available.

The cost depends on conditions. Pushing forward on site pays when the other side changes their mind mid-meeting, provided the trip is mainly reconnaissance and errors are cheap; the cost is arriving to find they wanted a written proposal. Preparing from the record pays in solid answers, provided this client resembles the last; the cost is that the focus has shifted and the preparation is aimed at the wrong thing.

The counterexamples hold as well: an ESTP who has dealt with public-sector clients often brings the full pack, and an ISTJ going to see an old acquaintance may take only a business card — the requirement of the duty outweighs the preference.

One thing worth doing is a review, not a change of method: after the trip, each writes three lines on what was mainly relied on, why it was chosen, and how they would adjust if the client moved the date or the requirement. The difference usually shows in those three lines, not in the size of the bag; and there is no need to repeat the trip several times to settle it.

### Packing to move: one van, the same two pairs of hands

(Fictional scene.) The lease ends and the move must finish on Saturday. One small van, two friends helping, a lift in the building, but the van can only park for ten minutes. The constraint is the same for both.

In this fictional scene, one approach handles the flow on the day: which trip takes the large items, how to stagger the lift, what can be bought after arriving at the new place; a box marked "kitchen" or "misc" is enough to recognise. The other handles the existing information: pack by room, number the boxes, write the contents, mark fragile items separately, load what will not be needed for six months first, and leave one "first night" box at the end. Both types can combine these bases; which step is taken depends on the division of work, the authority and the information available.

The cost follows conditions too. Handling the flow first pays in fewer van trips and a finish on the day, provided the large items are few and anything missing can be bought nearby; the cost is hunting through boxes for a pillow at night. Packing by room first pays in being able to live there immediately, provided there are enough hands and time; the cost is packing until dawn while friends wait downstairs.

A counterexample: people who have moved five times mostly label boxes, and someone living independently for the first time may shove things in anywhere. That relates to experience, hands and the day's energy, with no correspondence to four letters.

The real compromise is a division of work, not persuasion: one sets the van trips, the floor order and the route for large items, the other sets the packing rules and the first-night supplies, and who does which depends on who knows how and who is present. Before starting, both confirm two things — what time the van must leave, and which items must go in last — and the rest of the detail belongs to each.
sections.title: ESTP and ISTJ at work and in relationships

sections.body_md:
Reading E and I as "outgoing and lively" against "silent and withdrawn" is the easiest step to trip on. ISTJ can talk for a long time among familiar people, and ESTP can go a whole day without seeking anyone out. E and I describe whether attention and energy go outward or inward more often, not social appetite and not expressive ability.

The second misread is taking J and P as "has a plan" and "has none". ESTP will also work out the last train when travelling far, and ISTJ's weekend may have nothing arranged at all. The difference is whether an arrangement is formed outward first or options are kept, not the density of the calendar.

The third slip is ranking by "reliability", or reducing the shared S and T to "only wants data, only gives results". Punctuality, delivery and answering messages belong to habit and responsibility; both types can do all three and both can miss. Both types also cite data and both accept someone else's experience-based judgement; the difference is which is taken first. Using one incident or one catchphrase to overturn a whole set of preferences only describes how someone has been lately.
sections.title: ESTP and ISTJ: avoiding misreads

sections.body_md:
When two results differ, confirm whether it was the same questionnaire, version and language, then which kind of scene you had in mind when answering: a field or site role easily brings up specific handling, and a checking or record-keeping role easily brings up process and records. The requirements of a post shape the scenes called on while answering; that is not the same as a change of preference.

Only when the tool explicitly reports dimension scales and a threshold range should a near-boundary result be interpreted by its notes; without that information, do not infer a boundary, and no retest interval is prescribed. Turn the practice into a review: take three recent matters and write three lines for each — what information was mainly relied on, which standard weighed it, and whether a change in hands, deadline or risk would change the approach. If "what I saw on site" or "how it was done before" keeps recurring, that is worth discussing as your sourcing habit; it is reflection material, not a typing rule.
sections.title: ESTP and ISTJ: how to keep observing

items.answer:
Because the two differing letters flip the direction of all four positions while the category at each position stays the same.

ESTP's P makes the outward process perceiving, and an E type puts it in the dominant, giving Se with Ti auxiliary; ISTJ's J makes the outward process judging, and for an I type the outward judgement sits in the auxiliary, giving Te with Si dominant; under the four-position convention used here, the remaining pairs are Fe and Fi, then Ni and Ne. This whole arrangement is a convention here, the third attitude is marked differently elsewhere, and a different version should be checked for its source.
items.question: Two letters apart — why are all four function labels different?

items.answer:
A trip-planning discussion can bring out the preferences they share: both types may look at actual times and costs (S) and apply the same criteria to each option (T). Those are examples of what someone might consider.

To explore the differences, look across situations where both people have the same information and decision authority. E/I concerns where attention and energy tend to go. J/P concerns how each person prefers to handle arrangements and open options. Checking records or speaking first on one trip does not distinguish the types.
items.question: Why are they often taken for the same kind of person in a team?

items.answer:
Yes. Improvising and writing a list in advance are both learnable, and sit on a different level from four letters.

Some ISTJs have reordered an entire communication sequence when equipment stopped suddenly (the handling after a stop still follows professional guidance and the manufacturer's process), and some ESTPs write a step card when training a newcomer. What can be looked at is not whether it happened but the reason: did the change come because the conditions on site shifted, or because the previous approach no longer matched the record. A single scene shows nothing; several comparable situations begin to mean something.
items.question: ISTJ also improvises, and ESTP also writes the list in advance?

items.answer:
More likely one asks "what is most urgent right now, and who is it stuck with", and the other opens the handover documents and the history.

That is only the sourcing order in the first days, and cannot be extended into output speed or stability — how fast someone clears a blockage, how soon they reach steady output, depends on the complexity of the post, who is guiding them, their authority and luck, not on type. To judge fit, look first at whether the post needs more on-site judgement or more execution against an existing standard, then at the person's experience and willingness.
items.question: In a new post, what would each attend to first?

items.answer:
Divide by "flow" and "list" rather than requiring both to pack the same way.

Who sets the van trips and the floor order, and who sets the packing rules and the first-night supplies, follows who knows how and who is present, not type. Before starting, both confirm two things: what time the van must leave, and which items must go in last. The rest of the detail belongs to each, and neither rewrites the other's boxes.
items.question: Moving house together, how do they avoid dragging each other?

items.answer:
Check whether the results came from the same questionnaire, version, language and scoring method. Then revisit E/I and J/P separately, using several comparable situations where you had a genuine choice.

Only when the tool provides dimension scales and a threshold range can one say an item sits near the boundary; without that, do not infer a boundary. A more useful step is to recall whether you were answering as the person at work or the person at the weekend, and to write one line for each of three recent real decisions: what was referred to, why it was decided that way, and whether a change of conditions would change the approach.

Statements about cognitive functions rest only on the pages above; no in-site entry is cited here.

Editorial fiction: the client trip and the move are editorial fictions, corresponding to no real person, household or company, used only to illustrate how to compare preferences, and constituting no advice on how to handle either.

Scope limits: the content is not for ranking ability, screening candidates or predicting relationships, and cannot predict whether a collaboration will go smoothly or who is better suited to a stretch of work; judgements involving safety and professional matters belong to people with the relevant qualification, following the process.
